meta.label: Ride-hailing
meta.attribution: These are the ways a person in the United States gets a ride without owning a car or waiting for a bus: the two national gig-platform apps, two apps that book an already-licensed taxi instead of a gig driver, a taxi hailed on the street or called directly with no app at all, two driver-owned cooperatives, a company that employs its own drivers, a service built for children and other dependents, two services built for disabled and older riders, a phone-only service for people without a smartphone, a shared shuttle run with public transit agencies, a transit agency's own on-demand zone, a free electric shuttle paid for by cities and advertisers, two public entitlements (ADA paratransit for riders with disabilities and Medicaid rides to medical care), and three driverless services. Public transit itself, meaning buses, trains and transit passes, is a separate decision on this site; this one covers on-demand, door-to-door rides. The core trade-off is price against how much of your data and history a company collects: the cheapest and most convenient routes are run by platforms that share ride data with advertising partners and, in Uber's case, paid a nine-figure settlement over a covered-up data breach, while the more private and driver-owned routes usually mean a smaller network and less company infrastructure behind you if something goes wrong. Sourced from company safety and privacy pages, the California legislature, New York City's Taxi and Limousine Commission, the Utah Attorney General, NHTSA's crash reports, recall register and exemption notices, federal transit and Medicaid regulations, CMS, the New York State Department of Health, and the transit agencies and cities that run these services; every score links its source and date. Not legal advice. Reviewed 2026-10. Dispute or correct any rating via Contribute.

criteria.label: Less data shared with advertisers or exposed in a breach
How the driver is classified, paid or owns a stake
Published safety record or driver screening
Reaches riders the standard apps miss

products.name: Uber
products.description: One of the two national gig-platform apps, booked entirely through its own network of independent-contractor drivers. Uber's own safety report and a fifty-state data breach settlement are both part of the public record in a way most other options here are not.

privacy.note: Uber's current US privacy notice says it uses rider data for marketing and advertising, builds interest-based audiences and 'instructs ad and marketing publishers to target these groups, or audiences, with ads,' and shares advertising or device identifiers, hashed email, approximate location and 'current trip or order information' with ad intermediaries including Criteo, Google, Rokt, The Trade Desk and TripleLift. It also lists data resellers among the sources of enrichment data such as household income range and purchasing behavior. Riders can opt out of ad personalization. Separately, in 2018 Uber paid $148 million to all 50 states and Washington DC for waiting a year to report a 2016 breach of about 600,000 drivers' data, including driver's license information (see the linked Utah Attorney General release).

labor.note: California law, as amended by Proposition 22, states that an app-based driver 'is an independent contractor and not an employee or agent' of the network company, as long as the company does not set the driver's schedule, require acceptance of specific ride requests, or block the driver from working for other apps or other jobs.

safety.note: Uber's third and latest US Safety Report, published in August 2024 and covering 2021 and 2022 (over 1.8 billion US trips), recorded 2,717 incidents across the most serious categories of sexual assault and misconduct, 'a decrease of 22% in the rate of reports compared with our second Safety Report.' It also recorded 153 motor vehicle fatalities, a rate of 0.87 per 100 million vehicle miles against a national 1.35 but up 40 percent on the prior period, and 36 physical assault fatalities, a rate up 96 percent.

links.label: Utah Attorney General: Uber $148 million breach settlement (2018)

products.name: Lyft
products.description: The other national gig-platform app, built on the same independent-contractor driver model as Uber. Lyft's privacy policy and safety report draw on the same kind of disclosure Uber's do, though the specific numbers and dates differ.

privacy.note: Lyft's privacy policy says 'we do not sell your personal information to third parties for money' and that 'no one can buy the personal information we collect from and about you,' but adds that Lyft shares personal information with ad and marketing partners such as Google and Meta for targeted advertising, and that this sharing 'may constitute sharing or the sale of personal information' under some state privacy laws.

labor.note: California law, as amended by Proposition 22, classifies app-based drivers, including those driving for Lyft, as independent contractors rather than employees, as long as the company does not set schedules, force acceptance of ride requests, or block drivers from working other jobs.

safety.note: Lyft's May 2026 safety data release, its latest, re-reports 2017 to 2022 across every sexual assault and misconduct category in the RALIANCE taxonomy. For 2022 it lists 615 reports of non-consensual touching of a sexual body part, about 1 in every 880,000 rides, 135 reports of non-consensual sexual penetration, about 1 in 3,990,000, and 910 reports of attempted touching of a non-sexual body part, about 1 in 600,000. Lyft says its next Safety Transparency Report will cover 2023 to 2025; it has not been published yet.

products.name: Curb
products.brand: app that books an already-licensed taxi
products.description: An app that books and pays for an already-licensed taxi instead of dispatching a gig driver. A rider can also use it to pay a driver they are already riding with, without having booked through the app first.

accessibility.note: In New York City, the Taxi and Limousine Commission lists Curb among the three TLC-licensed taxi e-hail apps, alongside Arro and Myle, and says 'TLC-licensed taxi E-hail app companies must offer an accessible option.' Riders can book a wheelchair-accessible yellow or green taxi in the app or by calling 646-599-9999, and TLC says drivers are trained and required to help riders in and out and secure their mobility devices. This is a New York City licensing rule, so it does not show what Curb offers in other cities.

safety.note: Curb says every ride is with 'a fully licensed, insured driver' and that it connects riders with 'professionally licensed drivers who undergo background checks, vehicle inspections, and insurance requirements mandated by local taxi commissions,' standards set by each city's regulator rather than by Curb itself.

links.label: NYC TLC: find an accessible ride

focuses: Also pays for a hailed cab

products.name: Arro
products.brand: app that books an already-licensed taxi
products.description: A second app that books an already-licensed taxi, in six US metro areas, with a specific no-surge guarantee and a small flat service fee on top of the city-set meter fare.

accessibility.note: In New York City, the Taxi and Limousine Commission lists Arro among the three TLC-licensed taxi e-hail apps, alongside Curb and Myle, and says 'TLC-licensed taxi E-hail app companies must offer an accessible option.' Riders can book a wheelchair-accessible yellow or green taxi in the app or by calling 646-599-9999, and TLC says drivers are trained and required to help riders in and out and secure their mobility devices. This is a New York City licensing rule, so it does not show what Arro offers in other cities.

economical.note: Arro says 'prices do not increase, regardless of weather, demand or conditions' because 'rates are set by the municipal jurisdiction in which the taxi company operates and not by Arro,' and adds a service fee of up to $2.00 for a ride booked through the app, which it says may be waived in some circumstances.

safety.note: Arro says its drivers 'go through extensive training and education and are locally licensed for your safety,' the same city licensing system Curb also relies on.

links.label: NYC TLC: find an accessible ride

products.name: Licensed taxi, hailed or called directly
products.description: Flagging a cab on the street or calling a local taxi company, the way people got a ride before any app existed. New York City's fleet is used here as the best-documented example: its medallion taxis charge a fare the city itself sets and are not booked through Uber or Lyft, though many now also work with e-hail apps such as Curb and Arro. Most medallions are leased to drivers rather than owned by them, and the city now runs a debt-relief program for owners after medallion values collapsed.

economical.note: New York City's Taxi and Limousine Commission publishes the metered yellow-cab fare: a $3.00 initial charge plus 70 cents per 1/5 mile or per 60 seconds in slow traffic, a 50-cent MTA surcharge, a $1.00 improvement surcharge, $1.00 overnight and $2.50 weekday rush-hour surcharges, a $2.50 state congestion surcharge south of 96th Street, and a 75-cent MTA congestion pricing toll in the Manhattan congestion relief zone, with a flat $70 between Manhattan and JFK. The TLC adds 'There is no charge for extra passengers, luggage or bags, or paying by credit card,' and the meter rate does not rise with demand the way an app's dynamic pricing can.

labor.note: New York City's Medallion Relief Program gives individual medallion owners grants of up to $20,000, and up to $9,000 more in hardship cases, to help them 'afford their medallion debt, so more owners can continue operating yellow taxis.' Most drivers lease a taxi or medallion rather than owning one, and a separate TLC rule caps what an owner can charge a driver who cancels a lease.

links.label: NYC TLC minimum pay rule for app-based drivers

products.name: The Drivers Cooperative
products.brand: driver-owned co-op, New York City and Denver
products.description: A ride-hailing cooperative operating in New York City and Denver, owned by its own drivers rather than by outside investors. It runs on an app like Uber or Lyft's, but the company is structured so members, not outside shareholders, keep what it earns.

economical.note: The Drivers Cooperative says it 'takes a smaller commission than Uber or Lyft' and that this lets it charge riders lower fares while members still earn more per trip.

labor.note: The Drivers Cooperative describes itself as '100% worker-owned': members hold ownership stakes and a vote in how the company runs, earn 8 to 10 percent more per trip than driving for Uber or Lyft, and profits are paid back to drivers as dividends instead of to outside investors.

focuses: New York City and Denver only

products.name: Fare Co-op
products.description: A second driver-owned cooperative, operating in six states, and says it became America's third-largest fully licensed rideshare company less than a year after launching. Drivers can join as fractional owners for free or buy a full share for a bigger cut of the profit.

economical.note: Fare Co-op advertises 'no surge pricing' and says riders 'save 20% on average' compared with Uber.

labor.note: Fare Co-op says drivers 'hold 50% of the ownership, not Wall Street, not venture capital.' Fractional members keep 55 percent of platform profits on their rides, rising to 85 percent through referrals, and full shareholders keep 85 to 90 percent plus a co-op share.

products.name: Alto
products.description: A ride service that employs its own drivers and owns its own fleet instead of contracting with independent drivers in their own cars. It runs in four US metro areas, and in two of them its cars and W-2 drivers also appear inside the Uber app under Uber's own premium tiers.

labor.note: Alto says its drivers are 'W-2 drivers... not gig workers, with hourly pay, benefits, and opportunities for career development,' background checked, trained and continuously coached rather than engaged as independent contractors.

safety.note: Alto says its W-2 employee drivers 'are background checked, trained and continuously coached, plus AI-powered real-time video monitoring tracks performance,' and that it operates in Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Los Angeles and Miami, with its cars and drivers also running on Uber Black, Uber XL and UberTeen in Los Angeles and Miami.

products.name: HopSkipDrive
products.brand: booked by a guardian, for children and dependents
products.description: A ride service built for children and other dependents who need extra supervision, booked by a parent, guardian or school rather than by the rider. Its drivers, called CareDrivers, are vetted well beyond a standard rideshare background check.

safety.note: HopSkipDrive requires its CareDrivers to complete a '15-point certification, including background and driving record checks,' verified caregiving experience, and training in trauma-informed care and neurodiversity, on top of a standard driver background check.

products.name: Waymo One
products.description: A fully driverless ride-hailing service, so there is no human driver to classify, pay or vet. It runs in five US metro areas and publishes more detailed safety data than anything else compared here.

safety.note: Waymo's own safety data hub reports 220.6 million rider-only miles driven through March 2026, with 94 percent fewer crashes causing serious injury or worse, 82 percent fewer injury-causing crashes and 82 percent fewer airbag-deployment crashes than a human-driving benchmark, measured against police-reported crash data in the counties where it operates: Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Austin and Atlanta.

products.name: Via
products.brand: on-demand shuttle run with a transit agency
products.description: An on-demand shuttle usually not booked under its own name: cities and transit agencies run it under their own brand, such as Fort Worth's ZIPZONE, and riders share a vehicle with others heading the same way. It fills the gap between a fixed bus route and a private ride, at a fare set by the transit agency rather than by Via.

accessibility.note: Via says it works with '700+ partners across the world, from rural counties to large transit agencies,' running on-demand shuttles that 'fill the gaps' in a transit network. Named US examples include Trinity Metro's ZIPZONE program in Fort Worth, a Los Angeles Metro pilot connecting riders to transit stations, and an on-demand service in Jersey City linking underserved neighborhoods to public transit.

focuses: Booked under a transit agency's brand

products.name: GoGoGrandparent
products.brand: phone call only, no app needed
products.description: A phone-only service for people who do not want to, or cannot, use a smartphone app. Calling one number arranges an Uber or Lyft ride through a human or a touch-tone menu, at the underlying app's own fare plus GoGoGrandparent's own fee.

accessibility.note: GoGoGrandparent says 'everything works with a simple phone call. You don't need an app or internet access,' and that pressing 1 on the call line requests 'an Uber or Lyft to be sent to your home' with no need to speak to an operator.

economical.note: GoGoGrandparent says a caller 'pays the standard Uber or Lyft fare plus a small service fee for coordination, monitoring, and support,' so a ride costs more than calling the underlying app directly.

focuses: Costs more than the app it books

products.name: UZURV
products.brand: scheduled rides for disabled and older riders
products.description: A ride service built for people with disabilities and older adults, run through partnerships with paratransit programs, healthcare providers and transit agencies rather than sold directly to the public in most places. Wheelchair-accessible vehicles are available where a partner program includes them.

accessibility.note: UZURV says it provides 'safe, high-quality door-to-door service for older adults and people with disabilities,' including wheelchair-accessible vehicles for riders who 'cannot safely transfer to the seat of a standard UZURV vehicle,' operating through partner programs in cities including Houston, the DC Metro area, Phoenix, Jacksonville, Portland and Atlanta.

safety.note: UZURV requires drivers to pass 'national criminal and driving background checks' at least annually, complete Federal Transit Administration compliant drug screening, and complete credentialing on the Americans with Disabilities Act and 'appropriate techniques for assisting passengers with a variety of different types of disabilities.'

products.name: Zoox
products.description: A driverless robotaxi built from scratch with no steering wheel or pedals, run by Amazon's Zoox. It charges for rides on and around the Las Vegas Strip under a federal safety-standard exemption granted in July 2026, and gives free rides from a waitlist in San Francisco.

privacy.note: Zoox's privacy notice, last updated August 3, 2026, says it is not in the business of selling rider data, but it may use personal information for interest-based ads and works with third-party ad networks, sharing cookie and mobile ad identifiers and hashed identifiers; it says it does not share a rider's name or other directly identifying details with ad companies. It also lists in-cabin video, images and voice recordings among the data it collects. That is less than Uber shares (trip information goes to ad intermediaries there) but more than an operator that uses no ad identifiers at all. Riders can opt out of targeted advertising, including through Global Privacy Control.

safety.note: NHTSA's Standing General Order crash file lists 64 crashes reported by Zoox from June 2025 to July 2026, in California, Nevada, Texas and Florida. Most caused property damage only, and nine alleged a minor injury. Because Zoox publishes no mileage, these cannot be turned into a rate the way Waymo's figures can. NHTSA's recall register also lists five Zoox software recalls since March 2025, the latest (26E044, July 2026) because its software may fail to detect heavy smoke. On July 31, 2026 NHTSA exempted the Zoox robotaxi from parts of eight federal safety standards for up to 2,500 vehicles, with continuing operational oversight.

links.label: Federal Register: NHTSA grants Zoox exemption (July 2026)

products.name: Tesla Robotaxi
products.description: Tesla's driverless ride service, booked in its own Robotaxi app and run mostly with Model Y cars plus the two-seat Cybercab, which has no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla says it now offers rides in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando and Tampa.

safety.note: NHTSA's Standing General Order crash file lists 26 crashes reported by Tesla for its driverless service from July 2025 to July 2026, all in Texas. Most caused property damage only, two alleged a minor injury, and eight involved hitting a fixed object. Tesla publishes no robotaxi mileage or crash-rate data to compare with Waymo's. In September 2026 NHTSA also opened an audit (AQ26002) into how Tesla self-certified that the Cybercab meets federal safety standards (see the linked TechCrunch report).

accessibility.note: Tesla says its Robotaxi vehicles are designed to support various accessibility needs, with space for service animals and room in the trunk for some wheelchairs and other assistive devices, and that the app works with screen readers in 29 languages. There is no ramp-equipped vehicle for riders who stay in a wheelchair, and a smartphone app is the only way to book.

products.name: Circuit
products.description: Small all-electric shuttles that a city, transit agency or property owner pays Circuit to run inside a set zone, with advertising on the cars covering much of the cost. In most of its 40-plus US markets the ride itself is free. Riders book in the Circuit app, and in some places can wave one down or call.

economical.note: Circuit says cities, transport partners and advertisers subsidise the service 'so it's either an affordable fare or free', and that 'In most markets, Circuit is free thanks to our sponsors on the interior and exterior of our cars.' Some locations charge a small fare, and tips are optional.

privacy.note: Circuit's privacy policy, version dated May 11, 2026, says 'We do not use mobile advertising identifiers (such as IDFA/AAID) for app tracking or advertising purposes.' It collects trip details and precise location, may record video and, where the law allows, audio inside its vehicles, and shares data with payment processors and other service providers. The service is paid for by ads printed on the cars rather than by targeting riders through ad networks.

labor.note: Circuit hires its drivers as employees through its own payroll: an October 2026 posting for a part-time Driver Ambassador in Redmond, Washington offers an hourly base rate of $20 plus tips, with medical, dental and vision coverage only for full-time employees. That is a wage rather than per-trip contractor pay, but many posted shifts are part-time.

accessibility.note: In Redmond, Washington, the city runs Circuit as RedLink, a free pilot that connects to light rail. Riders who need wheelchair access select it in the app, and 'An ADA-accessible vehicle will be used to complete your ride', though the city notes the accessible vehicle was out for repair. Circuit's own FAQ says call-in booking and flagging down a car are offered in some locations, but service covers only small zones and riders must be over 16 to travel alone in Redmond.

links.label: City of Pompano Beach: Pompano Circuit

products.name: Transit agency on-demand zone (example: DART GoLink, Dallas)
products.description: Some transit agencies run their own on-demand rides inside set zones, booked by app or phone and paid with an ordinary transit fare. Dallas Area Rapid Transit's GoLink is used here as the example: it carries riders curb to curb within a zone or to a rail station, and now sometimes sends a Lyft or Uber car at no extra cost.

economical.note: DART says GoLink costs nothing beyond a regular transit fare: 'your valid contactless DART fare covers everything', including when the agency dispatches a Lyft or Uber car. DART's fares page lists a local 3-hour pass at $3.00 and a local day pass at $6.00, with daily and monthly fare capping in its GoPass app.

accessibility.note: DART says 'GoLink is available from 5 a.m. to midnight, 7 days a week' in most zones, can be booked in its app or by calling 214-515-7272, and that riders who need a wheelchair-accessible vehicle should request one when booking. Rides stay inside a designated zone or go to a rail station or transit center, so it does not cover cross-town trips.

products.name: ADA paratransit (example: Access-A-Ride, New York City)
products.brand: public transit agency, required by federal law
products.description: Every public transit agency that runs fixed bus or rail routes must also run a door-to-door shared ride for people whose disability stops them using those routes, at a capped fare. New York's Access-A-Ride is used here as the example. Riders must apply and be found eligible, and trips are usually booked a day or two ahead.

economical.note: Federal rules say the fare for ADA complementary paratransit 'shall not exceed twice the fare that would be charged to an individual paying full fare' for a similar bus or rail trip, and 'A personal care attendant shall not be charged for complementary paratransit service.'

accessibility.note: The MTA says Access-A-Ride 'provides public transportation for eligible customers with disabilities that prevent them from using the public buses and subways', across all five boroughs and nearby parts of Nassau and Westchester, '24 hours a day, seven days a week, including holidays'. It is a shared ride, and riders must first qualify. The MTA booking page says trips are reserved one or two days ahead.

products.name: Medicaid ride to medical appointments (NEMT)
products.description: Every state's Medicaid program must make sure members with no other way to get there can reach covered medical care, usually through a broker that books a van, taxi, rideshare or transit trip. It only covers trips to medical appointments, and usually has to be booked days in advance. New York's program is used here for the rider-side details.

economical.note: New York's Department of Health says its Medicaid Transportation program gets members to and from medical appointments 'at no cost to them', through a broker, Medical Answering Services. It adds 'We do not provide trips to non-medical locations like pharmacies, gyms, schools, or grocery stores' and that members should request a ride 'at least 72 hours in advance of the appointment'.

accessibility.note: CMS says federal regulations require every state Medicaid agency to 'assure necessary transportation for clients to and from providers', a requirement Congress wrote into the Medicaid statute in 2021, and that agencies must also help children in the EPSDT program with transportation. CMS's coverage guide describes this as a guarantee for members with no other way to reach covered care rather than a ride for every trip.

safety.note: Since 2021, federal law requires state Medicaid plans to ensure that every transport provider and driver, including rideshare companies, is not excluded from federal health programs, that each driver has a valid driver's license that providers have a process for drug-law violations, and that they disclose each driver's driving history to the state. That is a floor set by CMS; states and brokers can require more.

products.name: SilverRide
products.description: An assisted ride service for older adults and people with disabilities whose drivers can escort a rider from inside the door to inside the destination. Most rides are arranged through transit agencies, PACE programs and health plans, but families can also book directly by phone or online.

accessibility.note: SilverRide says it is 'licensed in 21 states and operating in more than 35 major metro areas', offers 'Sedan, SUV, and wheelchair-accessible vehicle options', and provides levels of help up to 'Door-Through-Door: an escort from inside the pickup location to inside the destination.' It runs supplemental ADA paratransit for transit agencies, and a family can book directly by calling 1-800-618-1246. A May 2026 trade report of its own press release gave 15 states rather than 21.

safety.note: SilverRide says 'all drivers undergo extensive background checks with the FBI and the Department of Justice', that 'Drivers are also fingerprinted and must have a clean driving record with the DMV', and that all drivers are drug and alcohol tested under Federal Transit Administration guidelines and trained to physically assist riders.

labor.note: SilverRide tells drivers they work 'As an independent contractor in the gig economy', choosing trips and discussing rates, the same classification as Uber and Lyft drivers. It says drivers typically earn more than at other rideshare companies and lists the minimum-earnings guarantees that California and Seattle require for contractors.
